restrictions: Generic memoryless collision search (Pollard rho with Floyd cycle finding) on the iteration map f(x) = H(enc(x)), where H is the complete sha3-256-r6-prefix-v1 hash and enc(x) is the 32-byte little-endian encoding of a 256-bit word x; each evaluation absorbs one block and makes one six-round permutation call.
Both colliding messages are distinct 32-byte strings; the full 256-bit digests agree.

Evaluations capped at 3*2^128 in the cycle-detection phase and at most 2*2^128 in the tail phase: at most 5*2^128 permutation calls plus at most 64 other word operations per evaluation (cost 1/1626 each) and a constant setup, so T <= 5*2^128*(1+64/1626)+64 < 2^130.38 target compressions.
Memory: the 25-lane Keccak state, three 256-bit words (x0, tortoise, hare), loop counters and code, below 2^16 bytes. No tables, no preprocessing, no advice.

Success probability >= 0.3934 - 2^-128 > 0.39 rests on one declared heuristic, H_random: from a uniformly random start, the trajectory of f has the first-repeat distribution of a uniform random mapping on 2^256 points. Nothing about the structure of six-round Keccak is used or claimed; this is a generic attack that improves the current incumbent's scalar score.

heuristics.statement: Let x0 be a uniform random 256-bit word (one call of the cost model's random-word primitive) and x_{i+1} = f(x_i) with f(x) = H(enc(x)). Let L be the number of distinct values x_0, x_1, ... before the first repeat. Assume Pr[L <= k] >= 1 - prod_{i=1}^{k-1} (1 - i/2^256) for k = 2^128, and that, conditioned on L = l, the repeated value x_l equals x_0 with probability at most 1/l; these are the exact values for a uniform random mapping. Then success >= 1 - exp(-(2^256 - 2^128)/2^257) - 2^-128 >= 0.3934 > 0.39 (proof.md Section 4).
heuristics.scope: The single trajectory of the full-width map f on 2^256 points from a fresh uniform start, up to 2^128 distinct points; complete six-round SHA3-256 on 32-byte one-block messages.
heuristics.extrapolation: The organizer-executed experiment rho-reduced runs the identical Floyd algorithm on the 16-bit truncation of the same f (2^16 points) and the organizer checks every returned pair agrees on digest bits 0..15 with distinct messages; under a random mapping every trial succeeds unless x0 lies on its cycle (probability about sqrt(pi/(8*2^16)) < 0.5%), and the mean evaluation count is about 2.5 sqrt(pi 2^16/2) ~ 800 (local run: 40/40 successes, mean 812). This is extrapolated to the full 256-bit width. Six-round Keccak-f[1600] is a nonlinear permutation of algebraic degree 2^6 with full diffusion after three rounds, and the best published collision attacks on 6-round SHA3-256 are not practical, so there is no known structure making the first-repeat distribution of f substantially worse than random; any deviation would have to shorten rho collision search, i.e. help, not hurt, unless f were far from random in a way never reported.
heuristics.limitations: An assumption, standard for generic birthday/rho analyses but not proved for six-round SHA3-256. The experiment reaches 16-bit truncations only; no 256-bit collision is observed or claimed. The attack is generic and gives no cryptanalytic insight into Keccak; it is submitted because its scalar cost (about 130.4) is far below the incumbent's 248.67 (time 122.67 plus memory term 126).
